summaries.example: Imagine a scientist who has learned every physical fact about seeing colors but has lived only where everything looks gray. When she finally sees a red apple, she may learn something new: what that kind of seeing is like. Philosophers disagree about what this new learning shows.
summaries.summary: The knowledge argument uses a story about Mary, a scientist who knows all the physical information about human color vision while living in a black-and-white setting. When Mary first sees colors, it seems that she gains knowledge about what color experiences feel like. The argument says that if she really learns something, then complete physical knowledge was not complete after all. This could mean that conscious experiences have non-physical features. Critics offer different replies: Mary may gain abilities rather than factual knowledge, she may learn an old physical fact in a new way, or the story may not establish that she lacked any physical fact. The debate therefore concerns both consciousness and the nature of knowledge.
key_ideas: The knowledge argument asks whether knowing every physical detail is enough to know how an experience feels.
Mary is imagined as a scientist who knows all the physical information about color vision but has never seen colors normally.
When Mary leaves her black-and-white room, many people think she learns something.
Some philosophers say she learns a new fact; others say she gains abilities, such as recognizing or imagining colors, or becomes directly familiar with color experiences.
The argument is meant to challenge physicalism, but its conclusion depends on difficult questions about knowledge and concepts.
summaries.why_it_matters: The argument helps us ask whether a scientific description captures everything about conscious life. It also shows why two people can know the same situation in different ways: one may know its physical description, while another has experienced it directly. The issue remains debated because philosophers disagree about what Mary learns and what counts as physical knowledge.

important_terms.definition: The felt or experienced quality of something, such as how red looks, how pain feels, or how music sounds.
The view that everything that exists, including conscious experiences, is physical.
A carefully imagined case used to test an idea.
Knowledge gained through having an experience yourself, rather than only hearing descriptions.

questions_to_think_about: Could a person know every scientific fact about music without knowing what music sounds like?
Does having a new experience teach a new fact, or give a new way to understand an old fact?
Can someone imagine an experience they have never had?
What might Mary learn when she first sees red?

summaries.example: Suppose Mary has mastered every physical description of human color vision: wavelengths, retinal activity, neural processing, and behavioral responses. She has lived without normal color experience. After release, she sees a blue sky and forms a new belief involving the concept of that experience. The central question is whether the fact making this belief true is a new non-physical fact, or a physical fact she already knew under a different concept.
summaries.summary: The knowledge argument begins with an apparent gap between physical information and phenomenal knowledge. Mary is described as possessing complete physical knowledge of human color vision while lacking normal color experience. On release, she seems to acquire knowledge of what color experience is like. The stronger version infers that some facts about color vision are non-physical, challenging physicalism; the weaker version concludes only that some knowledge is not physical knowledge, which does not by itself establish non-physical facts. Responses divide into several families. The Ability Hypothesis treats Mary’s progress as practical capacities. The Acquaintance Hypothesis treats it as direct familiarity with a quality. The New Knowledge/Old Fact View accepts new propositional knowledge but says its truth-maker is a physical fact Mary already knew under a different, non-phenomenal concept. Other philosophers question the thought experiment, the meaning of physical facts, or the existence and role of phenomenal concepts. The argument may also be understood as a challenge to objectivism, the claim that an objective account can be complete. Its assessment remains controversial because it depends on theories of concepts, belief, experience, and fact identity.
key_ideas: The basic argument has two premises: Mary knows all the physical information about color vision, yet she lacks some knowledge about color experience before release. Its intended conclusion is that not all facts are physical.

The argument has a weaker epistemological reading, about kinds of knowledge, and a stronger ontological reading, about the existence of non-physical facts or properties. The weaker conclusion does not automatically establish the stronger one.
The phrase “knowing what it is like” may combine direct acquaintance with an experience and knowledge about another person’s experience. The entry distinguishes these stages.

Physicalists may deny that complete physical knowledge entails knowledge of every physical fact, deny that Mary gains propositional knowledge, or argue that she learns an old physical fact under a newly acquired phenomenal concept.

The dispute concerns whether phenomenal concepts are genuinely acquired through experience, whether they are physicalistically explainable, and whether they introduce a non-physical mode of presentation.
An alternative interpretation says the argument challenges objectivism—the idea that an objective description can fully capture reality—rather than physicalism itself.
summaries.why_it_matters: The knowledge argument tests a major claim about consciousness: whether a complete account of the physical world would include everything there is to know about experience. It also separates several questions often run together—what exists, what can be known, what concepts a thinker possesses, and what it means to know what an experience is like. For that reason, the argument remains useful even for readers who do not accept its anti-physicalist conclusion.

important_terms.definition: The felt or phenomenal character of an experience, such as the way a color appears or pain feels.
The view that reality contains no non-physical individuals, properties, relations, or facts; in this debate it is the target of the argument.
A position holding that some properties of conscious experience are non-physical, even if the rest of the world is physical.
Knowledge that something is the case, as opposed to practical ability or direct familiarity.
A concept applied to an experience from the subject’s own experiential perspective, such as thinking of a color as “this kind of experience.”
The view that Mary gains factual knowledge after release, but the fact was already physical and was previously known under another conceptualization.
The view that Mary gains abilities such as imagining, remembering, recognizing, or discriminating experiences, rather than new factual knowledge.
The view that some truths may be physical yet impossible to understand fully without having a relevant kind of experience.

questions_to_think_about: Does a new way of thinking about a fact count as learning a new fact?
Is knowing how to imagine or recognize an experience different from knowing that a fact is true?
Can physical knowledge be complete if some physical facts cannot be learned without a particular kind of experience?
Does the Mary case support property dualism, or only a limit on objective descriptions?
What would a successful physicalist explanation of phenomenal concepts need to explain?

summaries.example: Imagine a student who has studied every scientific detail about how the eye and brain process red light, but who has always seen only shades of gray. When the student finally sees a red sports jersey, she may say, “Now I know what red looks like.” One philosopher may say she learned a new fact. Another may say she gained a new ability to recognize or imagine red. A third may say she already knew the physical fact and only learned to think about it from a new point of view.
summaries.summary: The knowledge argument explores a puzzle about consciousness. Mary is imagined as a scientist who knows all the physical information about human color vision but has never had ordinary color experiences. When she is released from her colorless environment, it seems that she learns something about how colors look. The argument’s strongest form concludes that there must be facts about experience that are not physical, so physicalism is false. However, the source distinguishes this conclusion from a weaker claim: Mary may possess a new kind of knowledge without discovering a new fact. Several responses defend physicalism. The Ability Hypothesis says Mary gains abilities, such as recognizing or imagining colors. The Acquaintance Hypothesis says she becomes directly familiar with color qualities. The New Knowledge/Old Fact View says she gains factual knowledge using phenomenal concepts, while the relevant physical facts were already known to her. Philosophers also question whether the thought experiment is coherent and whether “physical knowledge” has been defined clearly. Another interpretation treats the argument as a challenge to objectivism, the view that an objective description can completely explain reality.
key_ideas: The knowledge argument is based on the intuition that a complete physical description may not tell someone what an experience feels like.
Mary’s case is designed to make this intuition vivid: she knows the science of color vision but lacks ordinary color experience.
There are two important versions of the argument. One concerns whether Mary has a kind of non-physical knowledge; the stronger one says that non-physical facts exist.
Some critics say Mary gains skills or familiarity, not new factual knowledge. Others say she gains factual knowledge, but about an old physical fact under a new phenomenal concept.
The expression “knowing what it is like” can be unclear. It might mean having an experience, knowing how another person’s experience feels, or knowing a fact using a special concept.
The debate can also concern objectivity: perhaps all facts are physical, but some cannot be fully understood without experiencing them.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate connects everyday experiences—seeing colors, feeling pain, hearing sounds—with large questions about science and the mind. It asks whether information about brains and behavior captures the whole of consciousness. It also teaches an important reasoning lesson: a conclusion about what someone knows does not automatically prove a conclusion about what exists. Philosophers must carefully separate knowledge, concepts, abilities, and facts.

important_terms.definition: The distinctive felt quality of an experience, such as the appearance of red or the feeling of a headache.
The position that all facts and properties are ultimately physical; the knowledge argument is often presented as a challenge to it.
An imagined situation used to examine what follows from an idea.
Knowledge that a statement or fact is true, rather than skill in doing something.
A concept formed or used from the inside perspective of an experience, such as the concept of how red looks.
The claim that a person can gain new knowledge while learning no new fact, because the same fact is understood under a new concept.
The claim that knowing what an experience is like consists mainly of abilities to imagine, remember, recognize, or discriminate it.

questions_to_think_about: If someone knows all the science of taste but has never tasted sugar, is there something they do not know?
What is the difference between learning a new fact and learning a new way to think about a fact?
Are abilities such as imagining and recognizing kinds of experience enough to explain Mary’s change?
Does Mary’s story challenge physicalism, or only the idea that objective descriptions are complete?
Which part of the argument seems strongest, and which premise seems most doubtful?
